15481-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers edited this Edinburgh journal number, dated Saturday, February 7, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with Up the Indus, a soldier's plain account of a river journey in India. The writer, a non-commissioned officer of ordnance, traveled from Kurachee toward Roree to join a siege train for Mooltan, ending at Sukkur instead.

He saw some three or four hundred miles of a river unlike others in India, and he tells only what he saw, without books or official sources. That modesty is the piece's charm: a working soldier's view of boats, banks, and towns on the way to war. The number as a whole offers the Chambers mix of travel, fact, and moral reading, made for readers who had little time but wanted the world brought home.
15549-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers edited this Edinburgh journal number, dated Saturday, February 14, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with The Pattern Nation, an essay on France as a country that volunteers experiments in government for mankind's benefit. France tries one form after another, each supposed to be right, then tries something else when it fails.

The essay warns that French projects are not always easy to lay aside, above all in land law. Changing a ministry at the Tuileries does little harm, but meddling with inheritance and the subdivision of lands reshapes property for generations. The number thus offers the Chambers blend: a topical essay, travel, and instruction, written for busy readers who wanted the world explained in short, clear pieces.
16924-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers edited this February 21, 1852 number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, new series, number 425, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with a trip to Venice, leaving Trieste by steamer on a bright September morning in 1851. The writers feared the famous city of the sea might prove overpraised, but they resolved to judge with candor as Alps, Adriatic green, domes, and pinnacles rose from the waves.

Chambers' journal mixes travel, tales, and useful knowledge in a cheap weekly for general readers. The Venice piece shows its plain, observant style, watching a city rise from the sea hour by hour. Readers who love Victorian periodicals will find a pleasant, varied number, best dipped into for its travel and its time.
16953-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers priced this February 28, 1852 journal at a penny and a half for a wide home audience. Its lead piece takes a fresh look at Robespierre, asking whether the feared leader of the French Revolution was truly the monster of common talk. The writer weighs five years of power, the scaffold lists, and the sudden end of the Terror at his fall.

More pieces in the same issue follow the journal's usual mix of history, life, and useful knowledge for plain readers. The Robespierre essay alone makes the number worth a look: it shows mid-Victorian minds testing a dark legend with care. As a whole, the issue is a fine sample of cheap, serious weekly reading in 1852.
28531-the-banner-boy-scouts-snowbound-or:
George A. Warren's The Banner Boy Scouts Snowbound, copyrighted in 1916, sends Stanhope Troop out on skates and iceboats. Paul, Jud, Bobolink, Jack, and their comrades of the Red Fox Patrol won their banner in open competition, and the troop has carried the name Banner Boy Scouts ever since.

Chapters follow the boys on the frozen Bushkill, through an ice-house collapse, a rescue, and an iceboat squadron's tour, into a blizzard, a wild dog pack, and the capture of hobo yeggmen. Warren writes brisk scoutcraft adventure, with first aid, snowdrifts, and forest cabins, for boys who loved the outdoors and the scout code.
34945-the-golden-web:
Anthony Partridge's novel, published by Little, Brown of Boston in nineteen eleven, opens under the heading A Life for Sale. A shabby caller with sunken eyes and trembling fingers stands hat in hand before a strong, bronzed man. The contrast between suppliant and master states the bargain before a word is read.

The contents of the two books promise the machinery of an Edwardian sensation novel: a purchase, a murder, a debt incurred, an imperious demand, and the question love or interest. Winifred Rowan and Ruby Sinclair carry the story's two poles, with Lord Nunneley frank in the second book and Winifred trapped before the close. Illustrations by William Kirkpatrick catch the confrontation scenes. Partridge wrote brisk, plotted fiction for the circulating library market, and this one spins its web of money and marriage as its title threatens.
366-bab-a-sub-deb:
Mary Roberts Rinehart tells this schoolgirl tale through Barbara Archibald, a sharp-tongued teen who calls herself Bab. Bab writes a school theme on her Christmas break, then keeps a diary of the scrapes that follow. She fumes at being a sub-deb, a girl not yet out in society, while her older sister enjoys full grown-up rank.

Bab schemes, fibs, and lands in trouble with teachers, guests, and a visiting celebrity, yet her voice stays funny and frank. Rinehart lets Bab plead her own case, full of pride and hurt in equal parts. The result is a light portrait of youth on the edge of grown life, eager to be taken as more than a child.
45866-the-spider-s-web:
The Spider's Web is a novel by Reginald Wright Kauffman, author of The House of Bondage, printed by Moffat, Yard in New York in 1913. Jean Paleologue drew the illustrations, and the frontispiece shows Betty at a window in the full light of a street lamp. Verses from Francis Adams, Whitman, and Swinburne head the book.

In an opening explanation, Kauffman warns off trespassers: his first four chapters were pronounced dull by his own book maker, on purpose. In 1909 he had projected a cycle of four novels, each separate in plot but carrying one view of life. The House of Bondage, The Sentence of Silence, and Running Sands are its other parts, and he wrote to convert readers, not merely to make art.
55304-azalea-s-silver-web:
Azalea's Silver Web, by Elia Peattie, was published at Chicago by the Reilly and Britton Company in 1915, with pictures by Kirkbride. Peattie had written Azalea, Annie Laurie and Azalea, and Azalea at Sunset Gap before it. The story opens as a letter from Tennyson Mountain, North Carolina, dated October 6, written by Azalea to her friend Carin, back at Vassar.

Azalea begs Carin not to like the Vassar girls better than her old friends, and reports how she and Annie Laurie keep polishing themselves at home. Annie Laurie will take extension work beside her dairy, while Azalea reads books lent from several hands. Fifteen chapters follow, through Madam Grandmother, Mallowbanks, a ball, a portrait, and a grandmother's story, to a close named Ring, Happy Bells. The novel belongs to the Azalea series of girls' books.
74188-the-web:
The Web is the authorized history of the American Protective League by Emerson Hough, published by Reilly and Lee of Chicago in 1919. The book is dedicated to the unknown Americans, unnamed and unrewarded, who made the history possible.

A statement in the front matter explains that the League was a vast, silent, volunteer army. It worked under the direction of the Department of Justice and its Bureau of Investigation. The opening pages print President Wilson's address asking Congress for war and the congressional resolution declaring it. They also print the Attorney General's thanks of the 1st of February 1919, spoken as the League dissolved that day. He says frankly that his department could not have done its wartime task without the League's help. The history that follows is, as the subtitle boasts, a revelation of patriotism.
bab-a-sub-deb:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote Bab: A Sub-Deb in 1917, a comic novel told as the diary of Barbara Putnam Archibald, called Bab. A sub-deb is a girl in the year before she comes out in society. Bab chafes at being treated as a child. Her older sister Leila, twenty months ahead of her, is treated as a young lady. Her diary records the injustice in full, capital letters and all.

Bab's schemes run from an invented sweetheart, borrowed to seem grown up, to family rows and school exile. A Christmas holiday full of incidents follows, which she feels bound to report. Rinehart, famous for mysteries, shows her lighter gift here. Behind the fun sits a sharp look at how girls of her class were raised.
britannica-1911-ackermann-johann-christi:
Johann Christian Gottlieb Ackermann (1756-1801) was a German physician born at Zeulenroda in Upper Saxony. He began medicine at Jena at fifteen under Baldinger, followed his teacher to Gottingen, and studied two years at Halle. Practice at Stendal, a factory town, from 1778 gave him original observations on the diseases of workers.

Translation made those observations count. Ackermann rendered Ramazzini's classic treatise on diseases of artificers into German, adding his own findings from factory practice. In 1786 he became professor of medicine at Altdorf, holding first the chair of chemistry and then, from 1794 until his death, that of pathology and therapeutics. He also wrote institutional works on the history of medicine and on general therapy.
britannica-1911-aurangzeb:
Aurangzeb, who lived from 1618 to 1707, was one of the greatest Mogul emperors of Hindustan. The 1911 Britannica entry gives him as third son of Shah Jahan, born in November 1618. His birth name Mahommed was changed by his father to Aurangzeb, ornament of the throne. Later titles hailed him as reviver of religion and conqueror of the world.

Deep religious feeling marked him from youth through his whole long life. Strict teachers of his faith shaped that bent in his early schooling years. Young commands beyond the Indus and against the Uzbegs tested his war talent. Mixed success there sent him south to the Deccan armies for new service.
britannica-1911-baumgarten-alexander-got:
Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten (1714–1762), a German philosopher born at Berlin, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A follower of Leibnitz and Wolff, he taught philosophy at Halle and at Frankfurt on the Oder, where he died. His claim on later thought is one clear act. He was the first to set up the theory of the beautiful as a science of its own.

Even the science's name is his. Baumgarten coined the word “aesthetics” for it, from a Greek root for feeling or sensation, a root the entry calls a flawed ground for judging beauty. His first work came before those of Burke and Diderot on the same theme, and Kant held him in great regard. The entry lists his chief books: the Metaphysica of 1739, the Ethica philosophica, and the Aesthetica itself.
britannica-1911-buhle-johann-gottlieb: Johann Gottlieb Buhle, who lived from 1763 to 1821, was a German scholar and thinker. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Brunswick and his schooling at Göttingen. He taught philosophy at Göttingen, Moscow, and Brunswick. Two of his books stand out. One runs to eight volumes, issued from 1796 to 1804. The other, on newer philosophy, runs to six volumes. It is praised as full and well written, but faulted for weak judgment.
britannica-1911-caleb:
Caleb is a figure of the Hebrew Bible. His name in Hebrew means “dog.” This 1911 Britannica article studies the traditions about him. He was one of the spies Moses sent into Canaan. The spies went out from Kadesh. For his courage, Caleb alone won a promise of land. Later tradition adds Joshua to that promise.

The article sets the accounts side by side. In one, Caleb drives the giant Anakites from Hebron himself. He offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes Debir. Othniel, his brother, wins her by the feat. In another account, Caleb asks Joshua for the promised mountain. A third account gives the captures to the tribe of Judah. A fourth gives them to Joshua in a great campaign. The article argues that Caleb began as a southern clan. Its seat was at Carmel, in the south of Judah. The genealogies later fold it into Judah itself.
britannica-1911-el-teb: El Teb, in the 1911 Britannica, is a short place entry on a halting place in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. It lies near the Red Sea coast, nine miles south-west of Trinkitat, on the road to Tokar. The entry exists for one grim event. On the 4th of February 1884 a mixed force under General Valentine Baker marched to relieve the Egyptian garrison of Tokar. The Mahdists routed that force in full, and the entry sends readers to the Egypt article for the wider tale.
britannica-1911-ernesti-johann-christian:
Ernesti, Johann Christian Gottlieb (1756–1802), was a German classical scholar born at Arnstadt in Thuringia. He studied under his uncle, Johann August Ernesti, at the university of Leipzig. On 5 June 1782 he was made supplementary professor of philosophy at his own university. On the death of his cousin August Wilhelm in 1801 he became professor of rhetoric for five months. He died on 5 June of the following year, 1802.

The entry is a compact life-and-works notice, and its second half is a list of his books. His chief works are editions of Aesop's Fabulae of 1781 and of the Glossae sacrae of Hesychius of 1785. His Lexicon Technologiae Graecorum rhetoricae appeared in 1795, followed by its Latin counterpart in 1797. His last work was Cicero's Geist und Kunst, published from 1799 to 1802.
britannica-1911-falke-johann-friedrich-g:
Johann Friedrich Gottlieb Falke is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a German writer on the past from 1823 to 1876. He was born at Ratzeburg in April 1823. He went to school at Erlangen in 1843. He soon turned to German tongue and letters of old times. In 1848 he moved to Munich for five years. There he used the state book store for his studies.

In 1856 he took a post at the German museum in Nuremberg. He kept its hand writ texts from the year 1859. With a partner he set up a journal on German culture. His own work stressed tax, trade, and sea power themes. Books on German trade and on the Hansa came from his pen. In 1862 he moved to the state vaults at Dresden. There he wrote on Saxon trade and tax past.
britannica-1911-fichte-johann-gottlieb:
Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762-1814) was a German philosopher, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens with his family and schooling. He was born at Rammenau in Upper Lusatia, the son of a ribbon-weaver whose line went back to a Swedish soldier of Gustavus Adolphus. The family was marked by piety, honesty, and firmness of character. Fichte added to those traits a heat and haste of temper taken, it seems, from his mother.

As a small boy he showed strong powers of mind and will. A lucky chance brought him to the notice of a local nobleman, Freiherr von Miltitz, who paid for schooling his father could never have afforded. After care from a pastor he entered the noted school at Pforta. In 1780 he went to Jena as a student of theology. He kept himself by private teaching.
britannica-1911-guichard-karl-gottlieb:
Karl Gottlieb Guichard (1724–1775) was a soldier and military writer. He is known by his Prussian name, Quintus Icilius. He was born at Magdeburg to French refugees. Leiden educated him for the Church. He even preached a trial sermon there. Then he abandoned theology for ancient history. A lost Utrecht professorship pushed him into the Dutch army.

He campaigned in the Low Countries in 1747–1748. Peace turned his learning toward ancient warfare. His Mémoires militaires sur les Grecs et les Romains appeared in 1757. Ferdinand of Brunswick sent him to Frederick the Great. The king kept him in his suite for eighteen months. A friendly correction over Pharsalia earned him his new name. As Major Quintus Icilius he commanded free battalions. He sacked Hubertusburg castle in 1761 on royal orders. He died a colonel at Potsdam in 1775.
britannica-1911-heineccius-johann-gottli:
Johann Gottlieb Heineccius (1681–1741) was a German jurist. He was born at Eisenberg on 11 September 1681. He studied theology at Leipzig and law at Halle. Halle made him professor of philosophy in 1713. Its jurisprudence chair followed in 1718. Legal chairs at Franeker and Frankfort came later. He finally returned to Halle in 1733. He died there on 31 August 1741.

Heineccius belonged to the school of philosophical jurists. He treated law as a rational science, not an empirical art. Expediency alone, he held, cannot ground legal rules. First principles run through all his doctrines. His Syntagma on Roman antiquities appeared in 1718. His Elementa juris naturae et gentium came in 1737. Turnbull translated that work into English in 1763. His son edited his complete works in nine volumes. His brother Johann Michael pioneered the systematic study of seals.
britannica-1911-hufeland-gottlieb:
Gottlieb Hufeland, who lived from 1760 to 1817, was a German writer on law and trade. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica praises his clear Kant based work. He was born at Danzig in October 1760. He studied at Leipzig and Gottingen and took his degree at Jena.

At Jena his talks on natural law drew large crowds. They raised the fame of that school in its rich years. Later chairs took him to Wurzburg and to Landshut. He also served four years as mayor of his home town. His law books state Kant rules with rare precision. In trade writing he built on Adam Smith for German readers. He first marked the boss profit as a class of income apart. His hint that rent is a broad term also drew note.
britannica-1911-spangenberg-august-gottl:
August Gottlieb Spangenberg was bishop of the Moravian Brethren and Zinzendorf heir. He lived from seventeen o four to seventeen ninety two. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Klettenberg, the son of a court preacher, he lost both parents young.

Orphaned at thirteen, Spangenberg went to school at Ilefeld in poor straits. He entered Jena in seventeen twenty two to study law at first. A teacher took him into his home and found him a grant. He soon left law for theology and took his degree in seventeen twenty six. Free talks on theology and work for poor children marked his Jena years.
britannica-1911-tennemann-wilhelm-gottli:
Wilhelm Gottlieb Tennemann is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tennemann was a German historian of philosophy, born at Erfurt in 1761. He was educated in his native town. In 1788 he became a lecturer on the history of philosophy at Jena.

Ten years later Jena made him a professor, and he stayed until 1804. He then moved to Marburg, where he held a chair until his death in 1819. His great work is a history of philosophy in eleven volumes. He began it at Jena and finished it at Marburg. The entry notes that he took Kant's theory as a kind of revelation. In 1812 he published a shorter history of the same field. That manual was translated into English in 1852. Readers meet a scholar who gave his whole life to mapping the thought of others.
britannica-1911-web:
Web, a word for that which is woven, gets a short word note in the 1911 Britannica. The word is shared by the Teutonic tongues and rests on a root for to weave. From cloth the sense spread to like thin forms in nature. It names the flat part of a bird feather that bears the barbs. It names the skin that joins the toes of water birds and some water beasts.

Most folk know the word best for the net a spider spins to catch its food. The old English name for that net meant poison head, the note says. In building craft the word can name the stone shell of a vault. That shell rests on the ribs and takes its curve from them.
britannica-1911-welcker-friedrich-gottli:
Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker, who lived from 1784 to 1868, was a German scholar of Greek and Roman studies and of old art. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Grünberg in Hesse. He read classics at Giessen and taught there from 1803. A year in Rome as tutor in the house of Wilhelm von Humboldt shaped his path. In 1809 Giessen made him the first chair of Greek letters and old art at any German seat of learning.

Clashes over his liberal views drove Welcker from Giessen to Göttingen, then to Bonn. At Bonn he set up the art museum and the library, and served as its first librarian. He travelled in Greece and Italy in the early 1840s. The article calls him a pioneer who tied the study of Greek art and faith to the study of Greek words.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agram-zagreb:
Agram, also Zagreb, Latin Zagrabia, is the ancient Croatian kingdom's chief see, in Austria. It was founded toward the eleventh century's end as Kalocsa's suffragan in Hungary, becoming an archdiocese in 1852. Latin Catholics number 1,319,367. There are also 118,304 Greek Orthodox, 9,573 Protestants, 11,929 Jews, and 1,877 Greek Catholics. Agram's 348 parishes have 615 secular and 66 regular priests.

The bishop's city of 20,000 lies pleasantly in a broad plain near the Save, ringed north and west by vine-clad hills. Its monuments are the archbishop's castle-like residence and the medieval Gothic cathedral and sacristy. Three suffragan sees depend on it: Bosnia-Syrmia at Djakovar, Senj, and Krizevac. The people speak Croatian. Agram has a southern Slav university, opened in 1874 chiefly through Bishop Strossmayer's efforts, plus a bishop's seminary, a boys' college, a Greek Catholic seminary, and a school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caleb:
Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite spoke for the tribe of Judah among the spies sent from Cades to scout Canaan. He and Joshua fought the gloomy reports of the other spies and nearly fell to the crowd's fury in the mutiny that followed. For their stand both were spared the decree that condemned the adult generation to die in the desert.

Caleb helped divide the Promised Land among the tribes and, at eighty-five, still in full vigor, claimed Hebron as his portion and took the field to conquer it. He last appears giving his daughter Acsah in marriage to Othniel. A second Caleb, son of Hezron and descendant of Judah, stands apart from him, and the first Caleb likely joined Judah by adoption rather than birth.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-423-volu:
Up the Indus goes the lead writer of number 423, dated February 7, 1852. He counts out a soldier's field rations first. Biscuit, salt beef, rice, tea, and arrack make the list. Then he boards a steamer at dark. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal lets the voyage narrative run at length, in a serving man's plain voice.

Helps's essays are reviewed, jelly-fishes described, and a steeple-jack's secret told. Arctic food gets a grave treatment through the record of Franklin's expedition, whose fate still hung over readers. The Artist's Sacrifice, accidents at sea, and American homage to Shakespeare lighten and darken the back pages. A poem to Wordsworth and a piece on intellect developed by labour end the week.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-424-volu:
France is the pattern nation of number 424, dated February 14, 1852. It is not held up for praise. The lead essay traces French troubles to one change. The Revolution divided property equally among children. That undid primogeniture, the old rule of the eldest son. Chambers's Journal draws a warning for British readers from the experiment.

A travelling companion tale and a piece on popular music, centred on Mainzer, follow. Readers also get a Newcastle newspaper of 1765-6, thoughts on employees and employers, and a genius for emigration. Small wonders earn their place too: the thinness of a soap-bubble is measured, and John Bunyan meets mince-pies in an anecdote. Forest teachings close the number.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-425-volu:
Venice opens number 425, dated February 21, 1852, with a traveller hiring a gondola, watching Byron's heroines in his mind's eye, and suspecting the gondoliers of overcharging. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal keeps the party on the water from the obelisk to the Leone Bianca inn, in a sketch half guidebook and half confession.

The great Afghan blunder then recalls a military disaster in cold print. Insects that survive astonishing ill-treatment, children suckled by wolves, and an electro-magnetic machine supply the curious facts. Colour in dress is treated as a science, Dibdin's sailor-songs are remembered, and village cleaning gets practical advice. Calder Campbell's poem By the Sea signs off the number.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-426-volu:
Robespierre and the wreck of France lead number 426, dated February 28, 1852: the essay lays the Revolution at the door of bankrupt finances, rotten principles, and a church disgraced by abuse. Chambers's Journal pairs that long historical reckoning with a character study under the heading Time's Review of Character.

Infant schools in Hungary show a gentler kind of national repair. The Losing Game, recent fire-panics, and partnership law bring the reader back to risk at home. A word to genteel emigrants warns one class of traveller in particular. Colours in ladies' dress, a shore-side meditation, and the cow-tree of Brazil, which gives a milk-like sap, close the week on three very different notes.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-fb:
A short Federal Bureau of Investigation report dated February 2003 sets out a model of the cell that carried out the September 11 hijackings. The bureau drew the model from the lives and acts of the nineteen men. Its aim was to help staff spot a like cell in time.

The report says the men hid in plain sight and kept to Western dress and ways. It traces Mohamed Atta as he sought a fresh passport, asked flight schools for training, and told friends he would study in the United States. One point stands out: at flight school the men sought jet skills such as turns and approaches, not takeoffs and landings. The report treats that narrow aim as a sign worth heeding.

A law enforcement sensitive summary of the PENTTBOM case, dated February 29, 2004, anchors this file from the Federal Bureau of Investigation. PENTTBOM was the bureau's probe into the September 11 attacks. The summary was made for field offices, which were told to send fresh facts to the team at headquarters.

The pages walk through the hijackers' last months in the United States. Sampled text tells of cross-country test flights in August 2001, with men flying out of the Washington area to Las Vegas and Dallas. It notes when men on one flight crew had still not taken their seats in the plot's last phase. Names, dates, and case codes fill the text, and the tone stays that of an internal brief.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: February 2001 gives this file its date in the Federal Bureau of Investigation interview records kept for the September 11 commission work. The pages that survive here are mostly deleted-page sheets. A name, Fahd, can be read in one line, with a note that he advised agents of something he had seen or heard. Past that, the text layer breaks down into codes and marks. The sum is small: an interview record from that month exists, most pages were withheld, and its substance cannot be read from what was freed.

Phone records drive this Federal Bureau of Investigation cable dated February 19, 2002. It went to New York's PENTTBOM team and to bureau posts in six foreign capitals. A warning opens it: phone numbers sent in from abroad had reached the bureau's phone database with gaps, and offices were told of the flaw.

The sampled pages then turn to Hani Hanjour and flight training in Phoenix. The bureau's theory was that he came in June 2001 for time on a flight simulator. Such a device would teach him to take a jet off autopilot and fly it by instruments to its target. Records from the school showed his use of an AST-300 device in April 2001. One page of the log, the cable notes, had been torn out.

A document request from the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks, numbered 23-4 and dated February 2004, forms this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. The commission asked for a copy of security system video said to show Mohamed Atta in Virginia in the first half of 2001. The packet lists videotapes as the item sought. The rest of the file, as freed, is forms and marks too garbled to read. No tape, transcript, or finding is in these pages. The file shows what the commission asked for, not what it got.
frontinus-stratagems-aqueducts-bennett-l:
Charles E. Bennett and Mary B. McElwain translated Frontinus for the Loeb series in 1925. One volume joins the Stratagems and the Aqueducts of Rome together. Frontinus was a Roman general, governor, and water commissioner of the first century.

The Stratagems gather hundreds of military ruses from Greek and Roman history. Generals win by deception, surprise, and psychology in his examples. The Aqueducts then gives his official report on Rome's water supply. The general and the engineer stand side by side in one author. Bennett founded the Loeb Classical Library's Latin series as its editor. The 1925 volume remains the standard English Frontinus for both works.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeShazoJohnWebs: John Webster DeShazo: the illegible handwritten document filed under his name - the OCR is unrecoverable. A ghost in the files, kept as is. Preserved as filed. An obscure item. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LebherzRichardS:
Richard Lebherz wrote a series for the Frederick Post on Fort Detrick, the Army's biological warfare center in Maryland. The first installment, 'A Deterrent,' ran on November 3, 1969. Its frame was larger than the base itself: Fort Detrick as a symbol of a national crisis over germ warfare.

The series appeared while public argument over chemical and biological weapons was reaching a peak. Lebherz wrote for the base's hometown paper, explaining the work to the neighbors who lived beside it. The first piece sets out the deterrent argument: that germ weapons, like nuclear ones, were held to prevent war by threatening a terrible reply.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Natio: On March 30, 2016, the National Security Archive launched the Cyber Vault, a website built to gather declassified and public documents on cyberspace, cyber conflict, and the governments that wage it. A news post from the Archive announces that launch. The project grew from a simple problem: records of the newest kind of warfare were being classified faster than historians could follow. The posting preserved here is the birth announcement of the collection whose cyber briefs fill neighboring shelves, a small document marking a long effort's start.
